notes.b: Weight training means lifting loads (weights) to make muscles work harder than usual. Heavy loads can injure you if you are careless, so safe habits come before any thought of lifting more.
points: Warm up before lifting, so the muscles are warm and ready for load, which lowers the risk of strains.
Learn correct technique before adding any load, because a poor movement with a heavy weight is how most injuries happen.
Breathe out on the effort of each lift (the hardest part, such as pressing the bar up), and never hold your breath.
Move under control, lowering the weight with the same care as lifting it, so the weight never drops or swings out of your control.
Use a spotter (a helper who stands ready to take the bar) for heavy pressing exercises, in case you cannot finish a repetition.
Check that the collars (the clips that hold the plates on the bar) are secured before each lift, so plates cannot slide off and unbalance the bar.
Increase the load progressively, one step at a time, rather than jumping to a heavy weight, so the body has time to adapt.
notes.tip: When asked how to train safely, give several specific habits from this list, such as warm-up, technique first, spotter, collars and progressive loading, rather than just saying 'be careful'.

notes.b: Pushing exercises move a load away from your body using the chest, shoulders and the back of the arm. Pressing and triceps extensions both train pushing, and in each the technique points protect the joints.
points: Pressing (bench press or shoulder press): the grip is just wider than the shoulders, which gives a stable base for pushing the bar straight up.
Lower the bar under control, because dropping it quickly wastes effort and risks injury at the bottom of the movement.
Press to full extension (arms straight) without locking out aggressively, so the elbow joints are not slammed at the top.
Keep the back flat on the bench, so the spine is supported and not arched under load.
Triceps extension (works the triceps, the muscle at the back of the upper arm): keep the elbows still and extend at the elbow only, so the triceps does the work and not the shoulders.
notes.tip: If asked to describe a pressing technique, include grip width, controlled lowering, full extension without locking out aggressively and a flat back on the bench.

notes.b: Pulling exercises bring a load towards your body. Rows work the upper back and curls work the front of the upper arm, and both depend on keeping the rest of the body still.
points: Bent-over or seated row (works the upper back): keep a flat back, so the spine is protected and the back muscles do the pulling.
In the row, pull the elbows back and squeeze the shoulder blades together, which makes sure the upper back is working at the end of the pull.
Biceps curl (works the biceps, the muscle at the front of the upper arm): keep the elbows fixed at the sides, with no swinging.
Swinging the body or moving the elbows lets momentum lift the weight, so the biceps does less work and the exercise loses its value.
notes.tip: Name the main muscle worked in a phrase only, for example 'a biceps curl works the biceps', and focus your answer on technique points such as flat back, elbows fixed and no swinging.

notes.b: The legs hold the biggest muscles in the body, and squats and lunges train them by lowering and raising your body weight, or a load. Good alignment of the knees and trunk keeps the joints safe.
points: Squat (works the thighs): feet shoulder-width apart and chest up, which gives a stable base and keeps the trunk from folding forward.
Knees track over the toes during the squat, so they do not roll inwards or collapse.
Sit back until the thighs are parallel with the floor, as if sitting onto a chair, which gives the full range of the exercise.
Drive up through the heels to stand, so the thigh and buttock muscles power the movement.
Lunge: take a long step, with the front knee over the ankle, so the front knee is not pushed too far forward over the toes.
Lunge: lower the back knee towards the floor, keeping the trunk upright, so the legs work and the back is not strained.
notes.tip: Give technique points in order, from starting position to the finish, and make them specific: for the squat, feet shoulder-width, chest up, knees over toes, thighs parallel, drive up through the heels.

notes.h: Loading for strength and for muscular endurance
notes.b: The same exercise can train different fitness components depending on how much weight you lift and how many times. Strength is the most force a muscle can produce, while muscular endurance is how long a muscle can keep working. Their loadings are opposites.
points: Strength: heavy loads with few repetitions, about 3 to 6 per set, and longer rests between sets (typical guidance), so the muscles recover enough to lift heavy again.
Muscular endurance: light loads with many repetitions, about 15 or more per set, and short rests between sets (typical guidance), so the muscles are kept working for a long time.
The two loadings are opposites: strength is the heaviest load for the fewest repetitions, and endurance is the lightest load for the most.
A set is one group of consecutive repetitions (reps, one complete lift), followed by a rest before the next set.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the difference between training for strength and for muscular endurance, so state load, repetitions and rest for each. Do not mix them up: heavy and few is strength, light and many is endurance.

notes.h: Core stability: what the core is
notes.b: Almost every movement in sport passes through the middle of the body. The core is that middle section, and keeping it stable lets the arms and legs work effectively.
points: The core is the group of trunk muscles, the abdominals (stomach), back and pelvis, that stabilise the spine, which means they keep it steady while you move.
Core stability supports posture, so you can stand and sit upright without slumping.
Core stability supports balance, because a steady trunk keeps your body weight over your base.
Core stability supports the transfer of force through the trunk, so force made by the legs passes to the arms, for example when throwing.
Core stability helps prevent injury, because a stable spine is less likely to be strained by sudden movements.
notes.tip: When asked for the benefits of core stability, give all four: posture, balance, transfer of force and injury prevention.

notes.h: Core stability: breathing, control, alignment and flow
notes.b: Core stability is a skill as well as strength, so core work is judged on how well it is done and not on how hard it looks. Four qualities show good technique: breathing, control, alignment and flow.
points: Relaxation and breathing: breathing is controlled, and the breath is never held, because holding the breath raises tension and stops the body relaxing.
Control: movements are slow and precise, so the core muscles do the work rather than momentum.
Control: positions are held without shaking or sagging, which shows the core muscles are strong enough to hold the body steady.
Alignment: the spine is kept neutral (in its natural curves, not over-arched or rounded), the head is in line and the hips are level.
Flow: transitions between exercises are smooth, so the body keeps its control as it moves from one position to the next.
notes.tip: If asked how to perform core exercises well, cover each quality in turn: controlled breathing with no breath-holding, slow precise control, neutral spine with level hips, and smooth flow.

notes.h: Core stability routine and example exercises
notes.b: A core session is more effective as a planned routine than as a random choice of exercises. The example routine mixes exercises that hold a position still with exercises that move.
points: A routine is a planned sequence of core exercises, performed in one session, so every part of the core is worked in turn.
Example routine, in order: plank, side plank, bird-dog, dead bug, glute bridge.

The plank and side plank are held positions, where you keep the body still and straight, while the bird-dog, dead bug and glute bridge are moving exercises, where the limbs or hips move while the trunk stays steady.
notes.tip: When asked for a core routine, list exercises in a clear order, such as plank, side plank, bird-dog, dead bug and glute bridge, and say which are held and which are moving.

notes.h: Circuit training: themes, equipment and intervals
notes.b: Circuit training moves you round a set of exercise stations, which makes one session train several things at once. A circuit is built from three choices: its theme, its equipment and its work-recovery intervals.
points: Circuit training is a series of stations (places where one exercise is done), each worked in turn.
Themes: muscular endurance, cardio, or sport-specific skills; the exercises at each station match the theme, so the circuit trains what the performer needs.
Equipment: body weight, medicine balls (weighted balls), kettlebells (weights with a handle) or steps, so a circuit can be run with little or no equipment.
Work-recovery intervals (typical guidance): 30 seconds of work, then 30 seconds of rest at each station, so the effort is repeatable across the whole circuit.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to use circuit or weight training to improve a named component. Say the theme (for example muscular endurance), the exercises at the stations and the work-recovery interval.

notes.h: Designing a circuit, with an example for a games player
notes.b: A well-designed circuit lets you keep working without tiring one muscle group too early, and it can be made harder as you get fitter. The example circuit shows these principles for a games player.
points: Alternate muscle groups between stations (upper body, lower body, core and cardio), so each group recovers while the others work.
Use 8 to 10 stations (typical guidance), enough to give variety and a full session.
Set the number of circuits to complete, which fixes the total amount of work in the session.
Progress by increasing the work time, reducing the rest, or adding circuits, so the body keeps being challenged as it adapts (the principle of progression).
Illustrative example circuit for a games player, in order: squats, press-ups, plank, step-ups onto a step, lunges, medicine-ball throws, side plank and passes against a wall.
notes.tip: When asked to design a circuit, alternate the muscle groups and say why, give the number of stations and circuits, and show how you would progress it by more work, less rest or more circuits.

questions.prompt: Describe how weight training and circuit training could be used to improve muscular endurance in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: soccer. Weight training: use light loads with many repetitions, about 15 or more per set, and short rests between sets, so the muscles keep working for longer. Choose exercises that match the leg and trunk demands of the game, such as squats and lunges, and add repetitions over successive weeks before adding load. Circuit training: set up stations themed on muscular endurance, using body weight or steps, with work and rest intervals of typically 30 seconds of work and 30 seconds of rest at each station. Alternate upper-body, lower-body, core and cardio stations so each group recovers, and progress by reducing the rest or adding circuits. Together the weight and circuit work build endurance in the muscles the game uses.

questions.prompt: Give two key technique points for a squat and explain why each matters.
questions.model: 1. Knees track over the toes: keeping the knees in line with the toes keeps the knee joint in a safe line, so it does not take twisting force under load. 2. Chest up: keeping the chest up holds the trunk upright and the back in a stable, neutral position, so the load goes through the legs rather than the lower back.
